newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan flexes new arms for pre-handover war games.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan flexes new arms for pre-handover war games.

text.p: Commanders on Tuesday displayed a broad array of advanced arms that will be put to test in Taiwan's biggest war games in years -- on the eve of arch rival China's reabsorption of Hong Kong.

Sticking to a decision to hold the June 23-24 drills despite U.S. calls for a delay, Taipei insisted the manoeuvres carried no political message and were unrelated to Hong Kong's July 1 return to Chinese from British rule.
"An exercise is part of the normal operation of military troops," the defence ministry said in a statement.
"There should not be too much excessive speculation lest it blur the real significance of the exercise," it said.
On June 11, the U.S. State Department urged Taiwan and China not to stage military exercises during the sensitive run-up to Hong Kong's return to Chinese control.

Hong Kong media have carried unconfirmed reports that China would counter with its own exercises sometime in June, raising concerns that the final pre-handover weeks might see latent Taiwan-China military tensions boil up anew.
Beijing has not confirmed or denied whether it was planning to launch an exercise.

Taiwan's military showcase in southern Tainan on Tuesday featured the fruits of its recent weapons build-up -- from the F-16 and Mirage fighters bought from the United States and France to advanced home-made Skybow ground-to-air missiles.

All these advanced systems, as well as U.S.-made Patriot antimissile missiles and radar-evading "stealth" frigates from France, were being prepared for live firings and operations in the June 23-24 exercise.
Some would be test-fired on Wednesday, officials said.

Though Taipei maintains the exercise is routine, it has acknowledged that any military drill in effect has China as the imagined enemy and that the very need for a strong defence arises from the mainland's military threats.
Taiwan and China have been at loggerheads since splitting after a civil war in 1949.
Communist Beijing still considers the Nationalist-ruled island a renegade province that -- like Hong Kong -- must be brought under mainland rule, by force if necessary.
Beijing has used its own huge and increasingly sophisticated military might to drive that message home to Taiwan.

China held eight months of war games and unarmed ballistic missile tests near Taiwan in the run-up to the island's March 1996 presidential election, which Beijing suspected was a bid to pursue full independence.
China's sabre-rattling prompted Taiwan to cancel its own scheduled war games in 1996 to avoid heightening the already acute military tension across the Taiwan strait.
This time, Taiwan has refused to back down.

Analysts say by staging the exercise in June, Taiwan makes clear that it would refuse any attempt by Beijing to bring the island under sovereignty in the same way Beijing plans to rein in Hong Kong, a British colony for 156 years.
"Taiwan wants to make clear that Taiwan is not Hong Kong," military expert Andrew Yang told Reuters.
"It wants to tell Beijing that Taiwan posesses its own army and will never accept the 'one country, two systems' formula."
Under the model of local autonomy, China has vowed to allow Hong Kong largely to run itself and keep its capitalist system for 50 years after the handover.
Moreover, Beijing maintains the "one country, two systems" model can work for Taiwan's return to mainland sovereignty.
Taipei refuses, saying it would reunify only if Beijing launched democratic reforms and accepted Taiwan's exiled Republic of China as an equal partner in negotiations.
